lesson.title: Separable Verbs & Spatial Prefixes
lesson.subtitle: German prefixes ARE English phrasal verbs: aufwachen = wake up, zurückkommen = come back

hook.title: Phrasal Verbs Spelled Straight
hook.content: English phrasal verbs puzzle the world: give up, wake up, come back, take along. Why? Because English put the little direction-word AFTER the verb. German kept the older arrangement: glue the direction-word ON as a prefix — and when the sentence runs, let it fly off the back end. aufwachen is wake up, zurückkommen is come back, mitnehmen is take along, einschlafen is fall asleep. Every German separable verb is a phrasal verb you already own, written as one word and then split apart by the sentence like a bracket.

footnotes.title: The Stress Tells You It Will Fly
footnotes.content: Separable verbs stress the PREFIX (AUFwachen, MITnehmen) — that's how German speakers hear the split coming. Inseparable verbs (ver-, be-, er-) stress the root instead, and never split. Stress is the whole secret.

pattern.title: The Prefix Flight Path
pattern.content:
Dictionary form: aufwachen, zurückkommen, mitnehmen, aufstehen. In a sentence the conjugated root takes position 2 and the prefix flies to the very end: Ich wache früh auf (I wake up early). Wir kommen um acht zurück (We come back at eight). Ich nehme das Essen mit (I take the food along). In a modal bracket the verb stays whole: Ich will früh aufstehen — the trapped infinitive keeps its prefix, and the bracket swallows both parts. Du siehst gut aus — you look good (literally 'out': you look well-out!).

One Denglisch ladder, read it the German way first: Ich mache das Fenster auf → I open the window on → I'm opening the window. The middle line is word-for-word German — the particle lands last, exactly where English phrasal verbs say it out loud.
pattern.linguist_note: English used to allow this too: 'up' could follow or lead (he rose up / up he rose). The German pattern is the same spatial logic — direction first in the dictionary, direction last in the sentence.

exercises.prompt: Match each separable verb with its phrasal twin:
exercises.meaning: wake up, come back, take along, fall asleep
exercises.explanation: German prefixes are English phrasal particles: auf = up, zurück = back, mit = along, ein = in(to).

exercises.prompt: Which English is built the German way?
exercises.explanation: Read it the German way: 'I open the window on.' The prefix auf flies to the sentence end — the exact seat where English phrasal verbs park their particles ('wake up', 'give up'), except German does it in writing, every time.

exercises.prompt: Recall the earlier clues: which of these pairs is the outsider?
exercises.meaning: Recognize a familiar German word by choosing between earlier connection patterns.
exercises.explanation: Thin, thorn and thumb use TH → D. Hope → hoffen uses P → FF.

exercises.prompt: One prefix, three bases: what does auf- do to machen, nehmen and kommen — and what does an- do instead?
exercises.row_law: the base keeps its meaning — machen makes, nehmen takes, kommen comes, in every cell
exercises.column_law: the prefix decides the direction — auf- opens up, an- reaches on, mit- comes along
exercises.explanation: Across the auf- row the direction is the same (upward, opening, visible); along the machen row the base is the same (making). aufmachen is the cell where both laws meet — and English says the identical thing with 'open up'.
exercises.affirmation: You read the row and the column and the cell answered itself — that is the German prefix system working, not memory.

exercises.idea: you're telling your household your plan for tomorrow: you want to get up early
cues: Inside the bracket the separable verb stays whole: früh aufstehen — prefix included
exercises.meaning: I want to get up early

vocab_hints.note: no English twin — just learn it with the phrase 'früh aufstehen'

idea_parts: what? → aufstehen, whole and unbroken inside the bracket
exercises.explanation: Inside the modal bracket the separable verb stays whole: will opens, aufstehen closes — prefix included.

diagnosis.cue: Inside the modal bracket the separable verb stays whole: aufstehen closes it, prefix included. The prefix only flies when the verb runs the sentence alone.

summary.outcome: Use separable verbs with the prefix flying to the sentence end — and whole inside modal brackets.

use_example.english: I want to get up early.

summary.takeaway: Separable prefixes are your phrasal particles: auf = up, zurück = back, mit = along — stressed up front, flown to the end.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the phrasal verb mirrors — fifteen separable verbs matched to the phrasal verbs you already own.

twist.prompt: Same plan, but it's happening now: I want to get up early → I get up early. (Watch the prefix fly.)
twist.explanation: Without the modal the bracket splits: stehe holds position 2 and the prefix auf flies to the caboose — the flight path this topic named. Inside a modal bracket it would have stayed whole.

zumachen.shift_rule: K → CH + T → S / SS / Z

mitnehmen.context_translation: I want to take the food away / to go.

aussuchen.shift_rule: T → S / SS / Z + K → CH
aussuchen.context_phrase: Du kannst dir ein Buch aussuchen.
aussuchen.context_translation: You can choose / seek out a book for yourself.

aufwachen.etymology_derivation: Separable: auf (up) + wachen (to be awake/watch); wachen and wake are one verb — a shepherd 'wacht' the flock. [wiktionary]

zurückkommen.shift_rule: T → S / SS / Z + K → CH
zurückkommen.context_translation: We are coming back at eight.
zurückkommen.etymology_derivation: Separable: zu + Rücken (the back, cognate with ridge) + kommen — 'come to-the-back', the exact mirror of come back. [wiktionary]

schwan.context_phrase: Der Schwan schwimmt auf dem See.
schwan.context_translation: The swan swims on the lake.
schwan.etymology_derivation: From Old High German swan, from Proto-West Germanic *swan, from Proto-Germanic *swanaz, from PIE *swenh₂-, to sound. English swan is the listed cognate. [wiktionary]

vertrauen.context_translation: Trust is more important than money.
vertrauen.etymology_derivation: ver + trauen (to trust): the same Germanic trust-root as archaic English trow, to believe. [wiktionary]

füttern.context_phrase: Wir füttern die Enten im Park.
füttern.context_translation: We feed the ducks in the park.
füttern.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *fōdrą (Futter + -n) — dialectal English to fodder is the documented cognate. [wiktionary]
